title: service-lifecycle-operational-blueprint-2025
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary:
This blueprint describes a single, structured operational flow that SREs and service owners follow from service onboarding through steady-state operations to decommissioning. It standardizes SLO definitions, error-budget governance, capacity planning, runbook templates, incident evidence requirements, and the set of tooling integrations we rely on for inference-serving workloads. The intent is to reduce ambiguity when services (particularly model-serving endpoints) transition between teams and to make reliability economics explicit.

1) Purpose and scope
- Purpose: ensure consistent, auditable practices for defining and operating SLO-backed services across Redwood Inference (hosted, dedicated, and private modes).
- Scope: applies to any production-facing service that contributes to customer-visible inference latency/availability or billing (e.g., text generation APIs, embedding endpoints, reranking jobs, batch exporters). Excludes purely internal support tools unless they have a customer SLA.

2) High-level lifecycle stages
- Onboard (define owners, SLOs, traffic profile, initial capacity)
- Harden (run synthetic canaries, set telemetry, runbook authoring, pre-prod load tests)
- Operate (monitoring, error-budget governance, capacity management, monthly reviews)
- Evolve (rollouts, A/B experiments, model-variant pinning, quantization changes)
- Decommission (drain traffic, archive evidence, remove capacity allocations)

3) Roles & ownership
- Service Owner: product/engineer responsible for correctness and customer impact (primary contact for SLO changes).
- SRE Steward: long-lived on-call and capacity steward; maintains runbooks and headroom calculations.
- Platform Owner: maintains infra primitives (Autoscaler, Cache, Model Warm Pools).
- Incident Reviewer: designated SRE who leads post-incident evidence validation.

4) SLO and error-budget standards (required fields)
Each service must publish an SLO document with these fields before production traffic is allowed:
- SLO name (short)
- Objective (e.g. 99.9% success within 300ms P95 or 99.5% availability windowed monthly)
- Measurement signal(s) and query definitions (PromQL/Cortex query or SLO Ledger metric id)
- Time window for SLO evaluation (30d rolling, 7d canary window)
- Error budget unit (tokens/minute, percentage of requests, % latency violations)
- Owners and escalation path
- Related runbook id(s)

Required thresholds and governance:
- Initial production threshold: all new model-serving routes default to a 99.9% availability SLO (30d) and 99th-percentile latency SLOs aligned to product-class (interactive: P99 < 450ms; async/embeddings: P95 < 2500ms).
- Error-budget burn policy (example):
  - Green: burn rate < 1.0 -> normal ops
  - Yellow: burn rate 1.0–3.0 -> SRE Steward review within 6 hours, disable risky releases/canaries
  - Red: burn rate > 3.0 or cumulative budget > 50% used in 24h -> immediate mitigation: auto-throttle non-critical tenants, open incident ticket, schedule postmortem if recovery not in 2 hours

SLO measurement examples (text for copying into SLO doc):
- Availability: sum(status == 200)/count(all requests) over 30d rolling 
- Latency violation rate: count(latency_ms > target)/count(all requests) over 30d rolling
Include exact PromQL or SLO Ledger query and a synthetic canary mapping for each SLO.

5) Capacity planning & headroom methodology
Objective: express required capacity in three frames: baseline (steady-state), headroom (buffer for +99th percentile bursts), and emergency buffer (graceful degradation lane).
Steps: 
1. Collect 14–30 days of request profile: tokens/sec distribution, sequence length histogram, tenant-weighted percentiles.
2. Convert workload to GPU inference units using our internal cost model:
   - baseline_gpu = ceil(mean(tokens_per_sec * cost_factor) / gpu_throughput_profile)
   - headroom_gpu = ceil(baseline_gpu * headroom_multiplier) where headroom_multiplier defaults to 1.5 for multi-tenant hosted routes and 1.25 for dedicated lanes.
3. Add graceful-degradation capacity: reserve 10–20% of baseline_gpu (or 1 hot spare GPU for small services) to enable controlled fallback (lower-precision model, longer tail latency).
4. Autoscaling policy template (minimum):
   - min_replicas = baseline_gpu
   - target_utilization = 65% (tokens-per-second based)
   - cooldown_scale_up = 30s; cooldown_scale_down = 5m
5. Capacity review cadence: initial review at deploy, monthly headroom review, and after any significant model change (quantization, new tokenizer) or customer onboarding >10% traffic.

Capacity artifacts to attach to service page:
- Traffic profile CSV (tokens_s distribution)
- Cost model input sheet (gpu cost per token by sequence length)
- Simulated canary runs (k6/locust configs)

6) Runbook template (mandatory sections)
Every service runbook must include the following clearly labeled sections:
- Title & owners (service owner, SRE steward, escalation contacts)
- Symptoms (what triggers runbook)
- Quick mitigation steps (ordered, human-readable)
- Automated mitigations (throttle policies, failover routes, circuit breaker commands)
- Verification checklist (queries to validate recovery, expected metrics)
- Post-incident evidence template (attach logs, trace ids, token-sampling, SLO Ledger export)
- Rollback & rollback verification steps
- Links to dashboards, alert runbooks, and relevant RFCs

Example quick mitigation (short form):
1) Identify spike source: run query 'topk(10, sum by(tenant)(requests_total) )'
2) If tenant spike present: enable token-priority cap for tenant via Traffic Sculptor CLI: 'tsctl cap tenant <id> 0.3'
3) If P99 latency > threshold and GPU utilization > 95%: scale up warm pool: 'ci-scale warm-pool --service <service> --add 2'

7) Incident review and evidence standards
Purpose: guarantee reproducible, structured post-incident reviews that feed capacity, SLO, and product decisions.
Required evidence collected within 24h of incident:
- Incident timeline (machine timestamps, author)
- SLO Ledger snapshot and burn-rate graph for the incident window
- Relevant traces (Jaeger ids) and sampled request payloads (redacted) covering pre-failure and recovery windows
- Model-serving internal metrics: kv-cache hit rates, batch sizes, kernel-fallbacks, OOM counts, device temperature anomalies
- Autoscaler and scheduler events (scale decisions, eviction logs)
- Any config changes (git hash) and rollout IDs active at time of incident
Post-incident artifacts must be attached to the review doc and preserved for 90 days. The Incident Reviewer scores the evidence completeness: 3 (complete), 2 (partial), 1 (insufficient). Score <3 triggers an evidence-gap action item.

8) Operational tooling & integrations (standard stack)
- Observability: Prometheus + Cortex, Grafana (dashboards), Loki for logs, Jaeger for traces. Export SLOs to SLO Ledger for governance.
- Capacity orchestration: Capacity Orchestrator (internal), Warm-Pool controller, and Autoscaler service (ci-autoscale).
- Traffic control: Traffic Sculptor (priority caps, tenant shaping), Throttle Manager.
- Evidence collection: Incident Evidence Collector (samples requests, stores in S3 with KMS encryption).
- Experimentation: Canary Runner (k6 integration) and Shadow Mirroring pipeline.
Integration checklist for a new service: instrument metrics + labels (service, model_version, tenant), create Grafana dashboard, add SLO Ledger entry, wire up Evidence Collector sampling policy.

9) SRE governance & meeting rhythm
- Onboarding review: must occur prior to production(approval by SRE Steward and Platform Owner).
- Monthly SLO health sync: product + SRE to inspect burn patterns and upcoming capacity events.
- Quarterly capacity forecast: SRE, finance, product to align on committed capacity for Dedicated customers.
- Post-incident review: within 5 working days; corrective actions scheduled and tracked to closure.

10) Rollout & Decommission checklist
Rollout (must be followed for any model or infra change impacting latency/availability):
1. Create canary with 1–5% traffic and 7d observability window.
2. Run synthetic canaries for 24–72h with representative prompts (include edge-case prompt-set).
3. Validate SLOs in canary window and run headroom simulation.
4. Stage rollout increments (5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) with automated gate checks on burn rate and latency.
5. Record rollout id, config hash, and recovery commands in runbook.

Decommission:
1. Notify stakeholders 30 days prior (or per contractual SLA if Dedicated).
2. Drain traffic: set routing weight to 0 over at least 48 hours.
3. Archive SLO and evidence artifacts (90-day retention) and update capacity ledger.
4. Release reserved GPU capacity and mark for finance reconciliation.

Appendix: sample SLO table (text)
| metric | objective | window | owner | measurement_query |
| availability | 99.9% | 30d | @service-owner | sum(success)/sum(requests) |
| latency_p95 | P95 < 350ms | 30d | @service-owner | histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(latency_bucket[30d])) by (le)) |

CLI snippets and quick copies:
- Add SLO entry (SLO Ledger): 'sloctl create --service <svc> --name availability --objective 99.9 --window 30d --query "sum(status==200)/count()"'
- Throttle tenant: 'tsctl cap tenant <tenant-id> --pct 20'
- Warm pool scale: 'ci-scale warm-pool --service <svc> --add 2 --reason "headroom for traffic spike"'

Concluding guidance:
This blueprint is prescriptive where risk is customer-facing (SLO definition, evidence collection, capacity headroom) and advisory where teams need flexibility (autoscaler tuning, exact headroom multiplier). Service Owners should treat this doc as the single source of truth for lifecycle decisions and attach the required artifacts to the service Confluence page.
